Empirical Research Plan: Distributional Incidence of a U.S. $15/t CO₂ Carbon Price

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy type: “Other” – Static partial-equilibrium tax-incidence micro-simulation that combines (i) household expenditure micro data and (ii) sector-level CO₂ intensities.

Why appropriate:  
• The policy is hypothetical; no jurisdiction-level or time-series variation in a U.S. carbon price exists to exploit with DID/RDD/IV.  
• The question is incidence—how a uniform tax on carbon embedded in every good would be passed through to households of different incomes—so a forward-looking accounting approach is standard.  
• The CES + EIO-LCA pairing allows us to translate every dollar of expenditure into tons CO₂, attach the $15/t charge, and compute the added out-of-pocket burden.  
• The “causal” exercise is the mechanical comparison of two equilibria: status quo vs. status-quo-plus-tax, conditional on a set of well-stated pass-through and no-behavioral-response assumptions.  
Because the exercise is deterministic, the relevant “identification” issues are the plausibility of those structural assumptions, not parallel trends, exclusion restrictions, etc.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Treatment variable: Carbon-inclusive consumer prices, i.e. p̂_j  = p_j + τ·EI_j , where τ = $15/t and EI_j is the CO₂ intensity (t / $) of consumption category j.  
• Control (counterfactual) group: Observed 2003 CES expenditure pattern with p_j (no carbon price).  
• Unit of observation: household h (and, in alternative specifications, capita-equivalent h).  
• Treatment timing: instantaneous, hypothetical; all households “treated” simultaneously.  
• No geographic or temporal cutoff; thus no RDD running variable.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. 100 % forward pass-through from producers to consumer prices, uniform across sectors.  
  Plausibility: Reasonable for long-run competitive markets; we will bracket with alt. pass-through rates (80–120 %) in robustness.

A2. Input–output production structure fixed (Leontief); emissions intensities EI_j from 1997 IO table apply to 2003 household consumption mix.  
  Plausibility: Some technological change occurred; 1997–2003 difference is modest, but we will test sensitivity with BEA 2002 IO update where available.

A3. No behavioral response by households or firms (zero demand/supply elasticities).  
  Plausibility: Over very short horizons or for small price increases (<3 %) this is common; we will provide back-of-the-envelope adjustment using CES fuel price elasticities (e.g., –0.3 for gasoline).

A4. Budget shares of households stay constant after tax (no general-equilibrium income or wage effects).  
  Plausibility: Acceptable for first-order incidence; we will discuss wage-incidence in limitations.

A5. CES sample is representative of U.S. population once survey weights are applied.  
  Plausibility: High; BLS design ensures representativeness but we check by reproducing published aggregate means.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Mis-measurement in mapping 109 CES expenditure codes into 491 IO sectors → incorrect EI_j.  
 Mitigation: Dual mapping exercise (conservative and aggressive match), compare results. Use BEA bridge tables and disclose mapping file.

T2. Incomplete/heterogeneous pass-through (e.g., regulated electricity rates, imperfect competition).  
 Mitigation: Scenario analysis using sector-specific pass-through elasticities from empirical literature (e.g., 0.7 for electricity, 1.1 for gasoline); report range.

T3. Ignoring behavioral substitution biases upward the estimated burden.  
 Mitigation: Re-run model with price-elastic demand for the four most carbon-intensive goods (gasoline, electricity, natural gas, home heating oil) calibrated from the literature; show upper and lower bounds.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # Fast data handling
library(fixest)       # Regressions
library(ggplot2)      # Plots
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
ces   <- fread("CES_2003_micro.csv")        # HH-level expenditures, income, weights
io    <- fread("EIO_LCA_CO2_intensity.csv") # Sector-level tons/$
map   <- fread("CES_to_IO_mapping.csv")     # Many-to-one mapping CES -> IO

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2a. Merge CO2 intensity to each CES category
ces_long <- melt(ces,
                 id.vars = c("hhid","weight","aftertax_income",
                             "hhsize","numearners"),
                 variable.name = "ces_cat",
                 value.name   = "exp_dollars")

ces_long <- merge(ces_long, map, by = "ces_cat", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
ces_long <- merge(ces_long, io[, .(io_sector, EI_ton_per_dollar)],
                  by = "io_sector", allow.cartesian = TRUE)

# 2b. Compute CO2 embodied in each purchase
ces_long[, CO2_tons := exp_dollars * EI_ton_per_dollar]

# 2c. Aggregate back to household level
hh <- ces_long[, .(total_exp      = sum(exp_dollars),
                   total_CO2      = sum(CO2_tons)),
               by = .(hhid, aftertax_income, hhsize, numearners, weight)]

# 2d. Simulate $15/t carbon price burden
tau <- 15
hh[, carbon_cost := total_CO2 * tau]
hh[, burden_share := carbon_cost / aftertax_income]        # household-level
hh[, burden_pc    := carbon_cost / hhsize]                 # per capita
hh[, lifetime_inc := aftertax_income / numearners * 35]    # toy lifetime proxy

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main “Regression” — trend of burden vs. income
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# For illustration, run semi-parametric regression of burden_share on log income
est <- feols(burden_share ~ log(aftertax_income), weights = ~weight, data = hh)
summary(est)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness Check – 80% pass-through
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
hh[, carbon_cost_pt80 := total_CO2 * tau * 0.8]
hh[, burden_share_pt80 := carbon_cost_pt80 / aftertax_income]

est80 <- feols(burden_share_pt80 ~ log(aftertax_income),
               weights = ~weight, data = hh)
etable(list(Base = est, PassThrough80 = est80))
```

Additional checks to script but omitted for brevity:  
• Re-run using OECD equivalence scale (divide income & burden by √hhsize).  
• Stratify by region.  
• Bootstrap standard errors by PSU × quarter to respect CES survey design.

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
E1. Direction: The carbon price is expected to be *regressive* when measured against current *annual* after-tax income: burden_share declines with income.  
E2. Magnitude: Prior literature suggests ≈ 0.7–1.2 % of income for the bottom quintile and ≈ 0.3–0.5 % for the top quintile at $15/t. I expect a ~2.5× larger burden percentage in Q1 than Q5.  
E3. Switching to *lifetime* or *equivalised per-capita* income should flatten the gradient, cutting the regressivity roughly in half.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Accurate mapping CES ↔ IO sectors ...................... 0.7 (some ambiguity)  
C2. Emissions intensities reflect year 2003 technology ..... 0.8 (close but dated)  
C3. Pass-through assumption reasonable ..................... 0.6 (sector heterogeneity)  
C4. Behavioral responses negligible at $15/t ............... 0.6 (short-run only)  
C5. CES sample representative / weights used correctly ..... 0.9

Average score ≈ 0.72 → Overall validity: moderate; results should be presented with scenario ranges and clear caveats.
